# logconNMF

SPARSE NONNEGATIVE MATRIX FACTORIZATION · LOG-CONCAVE PROFILES

Log-concave NMF.\
Automatic rank selection.
=========================

A structured sparse nonnegative factorisation framework for ordered
multichannel data, combining automatic rank selection, hard log-concave
profiles, flexible likelihoods supporting different noise models and
simultaneous multisample models that do not require trilinearity.

[Get started
↗](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/log-concave-nmf.md)[Explore
the
methods](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/index.md)

R · Grouped L0 discovery · Penalised likelihood · Flexible multisample
sharing

![logconNMF hex logo with log-concave profiles and corresponding
spectra](logo-dark.svg)

[**Automatic rank selection**Score additions, deletions and fusions by
penalised likelihood to obtain the most parsimonious
rank](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/logconNMF.md)
[**Hard log-concavity**Component- and sample-specific chromatographic
profiles](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/algorithm.html#log-concave-profiles)
[**Flexible noise families**Gaussian, Poisson, quasi-Poisson, Negative
Binomial and Gamma
models](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/log-concave-nmf.md)

## Nonnegative matrix and tensor factorisation to separate overlapping peaks

Hyphenated chromatography is a demanding test case for structured NMF
and tensor decomposition. In GC–MS, chromatographic separation is rarely
complete: when compounds co-elute, the spectrum observed at one scan is
an additive mixture of their spectra. In matrix notation,

\mathbf{Y}\_{i\boldsymbol{\cdot}} \approx \sum\_{r=1}^{R}
H\_{ir}\mathbf{S}\_{r\boldsymbol{\cdot}} +
\mathbf{B}\_{i\boldsymbol{\cdot}},

where \mathbf{H}\_{\boldsymbol{\cdot}r} is the elution-mode factor,
\mathbf{S}\_{r\boldsymbol{\cdot}} is the spectral-mode factor for
component r, and \mathbf{B}\_{i\boldsymbol{\cdot}} represents the smooth
background at scan i. Recovering the latent components is therefore a
constrained nonnegative factorisation problem: model order must be
identified while chemically meaningful structure is imposed on both
modes.

Nonnegative matrix and tensor factorisation have a substantial history
in hyphenated chromatography. Important examples include
[MCR-ALS](https://doi.org/10.1039/C4AY00571F), [NMF applied directly to
GC–MS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.talanta.2004.09.017), [nonnegative
unimodal matrix
factorisation](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICASSP39728.2021.9414631),
[global parametric analysis of multiple GC/MS data
sets](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemolab.2008.10.004), [PARAFAC2 for
retention-time
shifts](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291099-128X%28199905/08%2913%3A3/4%3C295%3A%3AAID-CEM547%3E3.0.CO%3B2-Y),
and the PARAFAC2-based [PARADISe
workflow](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052), including its
recent [shift-invariant trilinearity
formulation](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.3501). These methods
established that multichannel structure can resolve co-elution and
recover spectra with less interference than apex extraction alone. For
the factorisation community, these data expose where unconstrained
bilinear models and rigid multilinear coupling become fragile: rank,
profile geometry, observation noise, background and between-sample
variation all interact.

### What standard formulations leave unresolved

- **Optimisation and chemical rank.** Bilinear and multilinear
  factorisations are nonconvex. Different starts can give different
  stationary solutions, while ALS algorithms may enter long *swamps* or
  stop at a poor local fit ([Boutsidis & Gallopoulos,
  2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2007.09.010); [Tomasi & Bro,
  2006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2004.11.013)). The number of
  components is usually supplied or selected outside the main fit.
  Useful diagnostics and automated classifiers exist for
  PARAFAC/PARAFAC2 ([Bro & Kiers,
  2003](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.801); [Johnsen et al.,
  2014](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.2575)), but require fitting and
  comparing a sequence of prespecified ranks.

- **Peak geometry.** Nonnegativity alone permits multimodal or jagged
  elution profiles. MCR-ALS can impose unimodality ([Bro & Sidiropoulos,
  1998](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291099-128X%28199807/08%2912%3A4%3C223%3A%3AAID-CEM511%3E3.0.CO%3B2-2)),
  but unimodality by itself permits shoulders, plateaus and irregular
  tails. A more appropriate peak-shape constraint would be
  log-concavity, which is stronger: when imposed on the positive
  support,

  \Delta^2\log h_i = \log h\_{i+1}-2\log h_i+\log h\_{i-1}\leq 0,

  which implies unimodality while still allowing asymmetric and
  long-tailed peaks.

- **Instrument response, background and noise.** Standard factorisations
  do not jointly estimate a constant or smoothly time-varying
  point-spread function (PSF) and a smooth nonnegative background. Least
  squares also imposes a constant-variance Gaussian working model. Ion
  production and arrival motivate count models, while detector gain,
  aggregation and chemical variability can produce overdispersion or
  approximately Gaussian intensities ([Ipsen,
  2015](https://doi.org/10.1021/ac503554u)). Although Poisson MCR has
  been proposed—in the NMF literature, the corresponding
  Poisson-likelihood formulation is known as Kullback–Leibler NMF
  ([Cichocki et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470747278);
  [Lavoie et al.,
  2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemolab.2016.02.006))—it is a
  specialised extension that has not been routinely used in the
  chemometrics literature and does not account for overdispersion.

- **Multiple samples.** PARAFAC assumes trilinearity: apart from an
  amplitude, each compound has the same elution profile in every sample.
  Shifted PARAFAC adds translations but not compound- and
  concentration-specific broadening or tailing. Classical PARAFAC2 is
  more flexible, but still requires \mathbf{H}\_s^{\mathsf
  T}\mathbf{H}\_s=\boldsymbol{\Phi} for every sample s. Retention shifts
  can preserve these cross-products; changing widths, tails and pairwise
  overlaps generally do not. Flexible and fully constrained PARAFAC2
  variants relax important parts of this restriction ([Cohen & Bro,
  2018](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-93764-9_9); [Roald et al.,
  2022](https://doi.org/10.1137/21M1450033)).

| Method (typical cited formulation) | Rank selection | Chromatographic profile | Nonnegativity | Joint component selection across channels | Optimal spectral sparsity | Noise objective | Multiple samples | Rank and scope in the cited formulation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [MCR-ALS / NMF](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.124.018)^(†) ([GC–MS NMF](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.talanta.2004.09.017); [unimodal NMF](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICASSP39728.2021.9414631)) | Supplied; external EFA/PCA diagnostics | Optional unimodality and other constraints, but no hard log-concavity | Both factors in standard NMF and NNLS-constrained MCR; optional in broader MCR | No | No | Least squares is usual; generalized KL and specialised Poisson extensions exist | Separate, augmented or shared-factor multiset fits | Chosen for the mixture or interval being resolved |
| PARAFAC / shifted PARAFAC | Supplied; external diagnostics | One shared profile per compound; shifted variant adds translation | Optional | No | No | Least squares in standard algorithms | Exact trilinearity, or sample shifts only | Chosen for the sample tensor or interval |
| [Classical PARAFAC2 / PARADISe](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052) | Usually supplied; multi-rank diagnostic automation has been proposed | Sample-specific profiles with a constant cross-product constraint; no hard chromatographic shape | Historically not on every mode | No | No | Least squares | Retention drift and restricted shape variation | PARADISe compares candidate ranks within each chromatographic interval |
| Flexible / [fully constrained PARAFAC2](https://doi.org/10.1137/21M1450033) | Supplied externally | Optional nonnegativity, smoothness or unimodality; relaxed/flexible coupling | Can constrain every mode | No | No | Least squares in the cited formulation | More flexible drift and shape variation, with an explicit coupling penalty or constraint | Fitted at the chosen order |
| [Shift-invariant trilinearity](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.3501) | Supplied externally | A shared peak shape up to translation; cannot model sample-specific shape changes | Can constrain all modes | No | No | Least squares | Retention shifts under shift-invariant trilinearity | Evaluated on low-rank windows; whole chromatograms still require many separate models |

^(†) When both factors are constrained nonnegative and each alternating
least-squares step uses nonnegative least squares under a squared-error
loss, MCR-ALS and standard least-squares NMF solve the same constrained
bilinear factorisation ([Camp,
2019](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.124.018)). **MCR-ALS** remains the
established name in chemometrics and is the broader framework because
its regressors and constraints need not be nonnegative least squares.

The cited chromatographic workflows choose rank for a matrix or
retention interval. In PARADISe, intervals are selected to contain
preferably fewer than six peaks. Baccolo et al. subsequently automated
the PARADISe workflow. The rank of a whole chromatogram counts distinct
compounds across all intervals.
[PARADISe](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052) · [Automated
PARADISe](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trac.2021.116451)

### Commercial GC–MS software

The vendor guides reviewed here do not specify a preset objective for
deciding whether a better fit to the original ion counts justifies
another compound, a more complex profile or additional fragment ions.
Users can set peak width, height, area and signal-to-noise thresholds in
AnalyzerPro. In MassHunter, the correlation window affects how many
neighbouring peaks are resolved. These choices can change the peak list.
The nine commercial workflows reviewed have no published result on these
16 chromatograms against which to compare rank recovery, false calls or
area accuracy.
[AnalyzerPro](https://spectralworks.com/2016/07/08/using-analyzerpro-in-the-metabolomics-workflow/)
· [MassHunter,
p. 27](https://www.agilent.com/cs/library/usermanuals/public/G3335-90243_Unknowns_Analysis_Familiarization-en.pdf#page=27)
· [Commercial software
comparison](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/benchmarks.html#commercial-gcms-deconvolution-software)

### What logconNMF adds to constrained factorisation

01 · GROUPED DISCOVERY

#### Grouped peak selection

Candidate peak positions are selected jointly across detector channels,
pooling evidence across mass channels rather than thresholding ions
separately.

02 · SPECTRAL SPARSITY

#### Optimal spectral sparsity

Within retained components, sparsity-promoting penalised regression
favours parsimonious ion support; final selection moves are checked on
every original channel.

03 · MODEL SIZE

#### Automatic rank selection

Score additions, deletions and fusions by penalised likelihood to obtain
the most parsimonious rank.

04 · PEAK GEOMETRY

#### Hard log-concave profiles

Every retained profile is nonnegative, contiguous and log-concave during
fitting—a stronger constraint than post-hoc unimodality.

05 · INSTRUMENT RESPONSE

#### PSF starts, individual final shapes

[`estimatePSF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSF.md)
estimates a constant or time-varying PSF for initialisation. The
constant blind-PSF model is a constrained lag-separable convolutive NMF;
each final compound occurrence nevertheless receives its own width and
tail.

06 · OBSERVATION MODEL

#### Background and noise fitted jointly

A smooth nonnegative background remains in the model. Flexible
likelihood families cover count-like, overdispersed and continuous
measurements.

07 · MULTIPLE SAMPLES

#### Shared spectra without trilinearity

Samples retain their original grids, shapes, locations and areas.
Monotone area-preserving time warps account for drift without
resampling, and compounds may be absent.

08 · WHOLE-DATA SCALE

#### High-rank full chromatograms

Sparse screening and local likelihood updates support full chromatograms
and large batches directly, with hundreds or thousands of components or
sample–component occurrences.

Structured PSF starts, grouped screening, original-channel refinement,
profile restarts and criterion-checked fusion reduce sensitivity to poor
starts. The time-varying PSF is locally rather than globally
convolutional, and the final factorisation does not constrain profiles
to shifted copies of a common kernel. The same formulation applies to
other ordered multichannel signals with nonnegative, single-peaked
components.

### Rank-selection objective

For ordinary identity-link count data, the original-ion objective is

J = \sum_s D\_{\rm Pois}(Y_s,\mu_s)/\phi_s + \lambda\_{\rm
eff}\left\[\sum_k(\\p_k\\\_0-1)+\sum\_{s,k}d(h\_{sk})\right\].

Each shared unit-sum spectrum contributes one fewer degree of freedom
than its number of positive ions. Each sample-specific log profile
contributes the dimension of its fitted piecewise-linear shape. Absent
profiles contribute zero. The same criterion checks changes in peak
shape, ion support and component count for one or several samples. The
fixed background basis stays unpenalized. Coordinate updates and local
support exchanges can reach a local minimum. The [mathematical
description](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/algorithm.html#conditional-count-objective)
gives the acceptance rules and the criterion used for other noise
families.

## Installation

``` r

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(c(
  "tomwenseleers/L0glm/L0glm",
  "tomwenseleers/logconNMF/logconNMF"
))
```

The R package includes the conditional Poisson and quasi-Poisson solver.
It fits the original ion counts with compiled C++ kernels and uses
OpenMP when available. Solver selection is automatic for the requested
noise model and memory settings.

## Log-concave NMF for single samples

This deliberately small cuticular-hydrocarbon window contains six
co-eluting components and is used to make the recovered factors easy to
inspect. It is not a scale limit: logconNMF runs efficiently on full
sample matrices with approximately 10,000–15,000 time scans or more. The
initial dictionary `X` places a narrow Gaussian point spread function
(PSF) at each possible peak location. An efficient
[L0glm](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/L0glm/) fit then selects the
best subset that can explain the multichannel signal, thereby penalising
most coefficients to zero. Equally, logconNMF provides
[`estimatePSFFromStd()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSFFromStd.md)
and
[`estimatePSF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSF.md)
to estimate the PSF and construct the most parsimonious corresponding
dictionary from either externally run standards, such as an alkane
ladder, or the sample chromatogram itself.

``` r

library(logconNMF)
data(gcmsData1)
Y <- gcmsData1
g <- convKernel("gaussian", 65L, list(sigma = 9))
psf <- estimatePSF(Y, time = as.numeric(rownames(Y)), standard = NULL,
  nwindows = 1L, precluster = 1L,
  control = list(kernel_est = g, maxiter = 0L))
X <- psf$X
fit <- logconNMF(Y, X = X, time = as.numeric(rownames(Y)), background = matrix(1, nrow(Y), 1L),
  family = quasipoisson("identity"), precluster = 7L,
  control = list(initial_relaxed = FALSE, fusion_passes = 0L))

fit$rank                         # estimated number of components
profiles <- fit$H                 # scans x components
loadings <- coef(fit)             # components x original channels
spectra <- coef(fit, normalize = "l1")
GIC(fit)
```

Using
[`estimatePSF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSF.md)
here applies the same boundary-aware, column-normalised PSF construction
as the high-level GCMSprime workflow. Consequently, these settings
reproduce the identical fitted profiles, spectra and background in both
packages; repeated fits are deterministic.

The columns of `profiles` sum to one, so each row sum in `loadings`
gives the component’s total fitted signal across scans and channels.
Grouping similar channels can speed up the initial search. The reported
spectra use every original channel. We selected this six-component
example after a sensitivity grid over Gaussian PSF widths and precluster
counts: among solutions with six factors and chemically plausible
retention times, it gave the best balance of low GIC, accurate apex
times, compact profiles and strong enrichment of the compounds’
diagnostic ions.

![Background-corrected ion traces in grey, six fitted log-concave
profiles and a 2 by 3 panel of recovered spectra for six co-eluting
components](reference/figures/gcms-data1-decomposition.png)

Background-corrected ion traces in grey, six fitted log-concave profiles
and a 2 by 3 panel of recovered spectra for six co-eluting components

The upper square-root display makes weak ion traces visible; the six
spectra below are shown as base-peak relative intensities.

### Beer volatiles: compound-specific log-concave peak shapes

A beer-headspace window provides a more demanding real-data example.
Narrow, partially overlapping volatiles occur alongside a broad,
strongly asymmetric acid peak. Instead of forcing one common PSF on
every compound, the final factors act as compound-specific log-concave
effective peak-shape functions: they can be narrow, broad or strongly
asymmetric while remaining nonnegative and single-peaked. The associated
spectra are estimated jointly from all 518 mass channels.

[![Beer-headspace chromatogram with fitted compound-specific log-concave
profiles](reference/figures/gcms-data2-traces.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.html#beer-volatiles-and-a-broad-acid-peak)

Observed ion traces are shown in grey; coloured curves show the fitted
compound contributions. Component 17 captures the broad asymmetric acid
signal without imposing its shape on the narrower neighbouring peaks.

## Simultaneous log-concave NMF for multiple samples

For related matrices, logconNMF performs **simultaneous NMF** in the
terminology of [Cichocki et
al. (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470747278), [Badea
(2008)](https://psb.stanford.edu/psb-online/proceedings/psb08/badea.pdf)
and [Lee et al. (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0048238):

\mathbf{Y}\_s \approx
\mathbf{H}\_s\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{a}\_s)\mathbf{S}
+\mathbf{B}\_s\mathbf{A}\_s.

Here \mathbf{H}\_s contains unit-area log-concave profiles,
\mathbf{a}\_s gives the component areas, \mathbf{S} contains the shared
unit-sum component spectra, and \mathbf{B}\_s\mathbf{A}\_s is the smooth
nonnegative background. Monotone area-preserving time warps model
retention drift and are taken into account as alignment and Jacobian
offsets without resampling samples on a common grid; components may be
absent from any subset of samples. This shares chemical information
without imposing PARAFAC trilinearity or the PARAFAC2
constant-cross-product constraint.

Grouped PSF regressions divide the core budget between independent
samples and native threads. The scheduler estimates how many regressions
fit in available memory, including Windows commit headroom. After those
workers exit, a single process shares the original ion counts and fitted
means. OpenMP updates elution profiles across samples. It fits each
ion’s shared spectrum and sample-specific background coefficients
independently, keeping a fixed component order within each ion. The
general identity-link solver can stream original-channel blocks from
disk.

### Automatic rank recovery on full chromatograms

The same 16 simulated chromatograms were supplied to every program. Each
contains **10,000 scans × 550 nominal mass channels** (m/z 30–579),
covering approximately 50 minutes. Together they contain **88 million
simulated ion intensities**. Each of the **1,000 distinct compounds**
occurs in eight randomly chosen samples. The design therefore contains
**8,000 positive sample–compound pairs**. Rank here counts the distinct
generating compounds across the batch, each with a time-local elution
profile in each positive sample. Of the compounds, 990 have
exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) peaks and ten have a rising
shark-fin profile with an abrupt trailing edge. Higher concentrations
broaden both types. The acquisition clock allows a smooth retention
shift of up to 2.93 seconds between the first and last injections and
approximately 2% variation in scan spacing.

GCMSprime, using simultaneous logconNMF, **recovered the true rank of
1,000 exactly** in **35.95 seconds per sample**. It recovered **8,000 of
8,000** compound occurrences and made **no false-positive calls**. The
recovered peaks included **80 of the 80 acid occurrences**. MSHub
returned **1,414 deconvolved components**, 41.4% above the true rank.
The other five workflows produce peak lists or aligned feature groups.
Their outputs do not define a common factorisation rank.

The 1,000 shared factors matched the 1,000 generating compounds
one-to-one across all eight occurrences of each compound. This is exact
automatic recovery of the chemical component count from 550 measured ion
channels. Scan order distinguishes compounds that elute at different
times, and each compound contributes a shared spectrum wherever it
occurs.

The largest exact rank recovery we found in a published benchmark of
conventional NMF with added noise was **150 factors**. Squires,
Prügel-Bennett and Niranjan selected that rank on a 1,000 × 2,000 matrix
using minimum description length. They also recovered 50, 80 and 120
factors exactly. The 16 full chromatograms here contain **88 million ion
measurements**, compared with **2 million matrix entries** in their
rank-150 example. The simultaneous fit recovered **6.7 times** as many
generating components from **44 times** as many observations. [Squires
et al., Figs. 1–2](https://doi.org/10.1162/NECO_a_00980)

Eswar et al. compared rank selectors on simulated matrices with true
rank 10, testing candidate ranks from 1 to 20. Under Gaussian noise only
cross-validation and singular-value hard thresholding ever recovered the
planted rank in their experiment. Cai et al.’s Poisson NMF benchmark
rarely extended beyond rank 10, with just one higher rank (30) among the
six they tested. [Eswar et
al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/BigData62323.2024.10825324) · [Cai et
al.](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.9934)

Chennupati et al. recovered seven planted factors in a one-terabyte
matrix using distributed NMF. Fu et al. tested nonnegative tensor rank
selection at true ranks 15–40. [Chennupati et
al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11227-020-03181-6) · [Fu et
al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/e21070632) · [Evidence for automatic rank
recovery](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/simultaneous-nmf.html#evidence-for-automatic-rank-recovery)

Fitting the 88 million observations took **35.95 seconds per sample** on
a 64 GB laptop with 16 logical processors. The sampled peak working set
was **6.8 GiB**. At the same throughput, 1,000 equally sized samples
would take about ten hours. The current joint count solver would need
more memory than this laptop has at that scale. [Measurements and memory
requirements for larger
batches](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/simultaneous-nmf.html#scaling-to-larger-batches)

| Workflow | Seconds/sample | Estimated rank (true 1,000) | TP (sensitivity) | FP | FN | Acid TP / 80 |
|----|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GCMSprime | 35.95 | **1,000 (exact)** | 8,000 (100%) | 0 | 0 | 80 / 80 |
| MS-DIAL | 16.02 | — | 7,728 (96.6%) | 11,685 | 272 | 73 / 80 |
| mzmine GC-EI | 6.92 | — | 4,202 (52.5%) | 185 | 3,798 | 29 / 80 |
| eRah | 25.94 | — | 7,172 (89.7%) | 5,615 | 828 | 70 / 80 |
| AMDIS | 28.99 | — | 7,878 (98.5%) | 9,122 | 122 | 80 / 80 |
| xcms + CAMERA | 4.22 | — | 7,261 (90.8%) | 890 | 739 | 31 / 80 |
| MSHub | 15.05 | 1,414 | 7,179 (89.7%) | 12,184 | 821 | 50 / 80 |

Among GCMSprime’s 8,000 matched occurrences, the median absolute
relative area error was **0.095%** and ordinary adjusted R² on the log₁₀
scale was **0.999982**.

[![Estimated and true areas in the simultaneous
fit](reference/figures/simultaneous-benchmark-area-accuracy.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/figures/simultaneous-benchmark-area-accuracy.png)

[![Accuracy of recovered shared
spectra](reference/figures/simultaneous-benchmark-spectral-accuracy.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/figures/simultaneous-benchmark-spectral-accuracy.png)

### Convergence behaviour

The blind fit converged to a solution very close to the simulated ground
truth. It recovered **all 1,000 compounds and all 8,000 peak
occurrences**, with a median elution-profile cosine of **0.999994** and
a median absolute relative area error of **0.095%**. GIC showed smooth,
monotonic descent over eight sweeps. Its final value differed by only
**0.19%** from that of a fit initialised with the true elution profiles
and run for the same eight sweeps.

[![Original-ion GIC over eight sweeps of the blind fit on 16 full
chromatograms](reference/figures/full-benchmark-gic-gap.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/figures/full-benchmark-gic-gap.png)

[Block-level GIC
trace](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/blob/master/GCMSbenchmark/inst/benchmarks/results/gic-trace.csv)
· [Final GIC
values](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/blob/master/GCMSbenchmark/inst/benchmarks/results/gic-gap.csv).

### Elution profile recovery

The examples are the EMG compound and the acid with the greatest total
true area in their respective classes. Both were selected from the
simulation before comparing any fits. Each occurs in eight samples.
Solid curves show inferred profiles, dashed curves show the true
profiles, and the eight absent true profiles coincide at zero. Colours
order the 16 samples by true area. Heights retain original total-ion
intensity per scan. The mean cosine in each example uses all eight
positive occurrences, with a missing recovered profile scoring zero. The
all-acid tally covers all ten acids.

## Choose a workflow

| Data and objective | Method |
|:---|:---|
| Estimate a common response shape from a standard or overlapping signals | [Estimate PSFs](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/estimate-psf.md) with [`estimatePSF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSF.md). The returned sparse design can use a constant or time-varying PSF. |
| Resolve components with individual shapes in one matrix | [Sparse log-concave NMF](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/log-concave-nmf.md) with [`logconNMF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/logconNMF.md). The tutorial covers rank selection, backgrounds and flexible noise families. |
| Share spectra across related samples | [Simultaneous log-concave NMF](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/simultaneous-nmf.md) with [`logconNMF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/logconNMF.md). Each sample retains its own scan grid, peak shapes and areas. Components may be absent from individual samples. |

For a known and common PSF,
[L0glm](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/L0glm/articles/deconvolution.html)
fits the sparse convolution model directly.
[GCMSprime](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/) uses logconNMF
for chromatogram files, retention-index calibration and library search.
The [algorithm and
theory](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/algorithm.md)
give the objectives, shape constraints and mathematical pseudocode.

## Selected literature

The comparison above draws on the following methodological and
chromatography-specific work.

**Matrix factorisation and curve resolution**

- de Juan A, Jaumot J, Tauler R (2014). [Multivariate Curve Resolution
  (MCR). Solving the mixture analysis
  problem.](https://doi.org/10.1039/C4AY00571F)
- de Juan A, Tauler R (2021). [Multivariate Curve Resolution: 50 years
  addressing the mixture analysis problem—A
  review.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2020.10.051)
- Camp CH Jr (2019). [pyMCR: A Python Library for Multivariate Curve
  Resolution Analysis with Alternating Regression
  (MCR-AR).](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.124.018)
- Gao H-T, Li T-H, Chen K, Li W-G, Bi X (2005). [Overlapping spectra
  resolution using non-negative matrix
  factorization.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.talanta.2004.09.017)
- Ang AMS, Gillis N, Vandaele A, De Sterck H (2021). [Nonnegative
  Unimodal Matrix
  Factorization.](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICASSP39728.2021.9414631)
- van Stokkum IHM, Mullen KM, Mihaleva VV (2009). [Global analysis of
  multiple gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC/MS) data sets: A
  method for resolution of co-eluting components with comparison to
  MCR-ALS.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemolab.2008.10.004)
- Lavoie FB, Braidy N, Gosselin R (2016). [Including noise
  characteristics in MCR to improve mapping and component extraction
  from spectral images.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemolab.2016.02.006)

**Simultaneous and convolutive NMF**

- Cichocki A, Zdunek R, Phan AH, Amari S-I (2009). [*Nonnegative Matrix
  and Tensor Factorizations: Applications to Exploratory Multi-way Data
  Analysis and Blind Source
  Separation*.](https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470747278)
- Badea L (2008). [Extracting gene expression profiles common to colon
  and pancreatic adenocarcinoma using simultaneous nonnegative matrix
  factorization.](https://psb.stanford.edu/psb-online/proceedings/psb08/badea.pdf)
- Lee CM, Mudaliar MAV, Haggart DR, Wolf CR, Miele G, Vass JK, Higham DJ
  (2012). [Simultaneous non-negative matrix factorization for multiple
  large scale gene expression datasets in
  toxicology.](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0048238)

**Tensor factorisation for chromatographic data**

- Bro R, Andersson CA, Kiers HAL (1999). [PARAFAC2—Part II. Modeling
  chromatographic data with retention time
  shifts.](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291099-128X%28199905/08%2913%3A3/4%3C295%3A%3AAID-CEM547%3E3.0.CO%3B2-Y)
- Amigo JM, Skov T, Coello J, Maspoch S, Bro R (2008). [Solving GC–MS
  problems with PARAFAC2.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trac.2008.05.011)
- Johnsen LG, Amigo JM, Skov T, Bro R (2014). [Automated resolution of
  overlapping peaks in chromatographic
  data.](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.2575)
- Johnsen LG, Skou PB, Khakimov B, Bro R (2017). [Gas
  chromatography–mass spectrometry data processing made
  easy.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052)
- Schneide P-A, Bro R, Gallagher NB (2023). [Shift-invariant
  tri-linearity—A new model for resolving untargeted gas chromatography
  coupled mass spectrometry data.](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.3501)
- Cohen JE, Bro R (2018). [Nonnegative PARAFAC2: a flexible coupling
  approach.](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-93764-9_9)
- Roald M, Schenker C, Calhoun VD, Adalı T, Bro R, Cohen JE, Acar E
  (2022). [An AO-ADMM approach to constraining PARAFAC2 on all
  modes.](https://doi.org/10.1137/21M1450033)
- Sorochan Armstrong MD, Hinrich JL, de la Mata AP, Harynuk JJ (2023).
  [PARAFAC2×N: coupled decomposition of multi-modal data with drift in N
  modes.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2023.340909)

**Shape constraints, rank diagnostics and statistical modelling**

- Bro R, Sidiropoulos ND (1998). [Least squares algorithms under
  unimodality and non-negativity
  constraints.](https://doi.org/10.1002/%28SICI%291099-128X%28199807/08%2912%3A4%3C223%3A%3AAID-CEM511%3E3.0.CO%3B2-2)
- Eilers PHC (2005). [Unimodal
  smoothing.](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.935)
- Bro R, Kiers HAL (2003). [A new efficient method for determining the
  number of components in PARAFAC
  models.](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.801)
- Boutsidis C, Gallopoulos E (2008). [SVD based initialization: a head
  start for nonnegative matrix
  factorization.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2007.09.010)
- Tomasi G, Bro R (2006). [A comparison of algorithms for fitting the
  PARAFAC model.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2004.11.013)
- de Rooi JJ, Eilers PHC (2011). [Deconvolution of pulse trains with the
  L0 penalty.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2011.05.030)
- Ipsen A (2015). [Derivation from first principles of the statistical
  distribution of the mass peak intensities of MS
  data.](https://doi.org/10.1021/ac503554u)

## Citation

An article describing the methods implemented in logconNMF is in
preparation. If you use the package before the article is formally
published, we would appreciate a citation to the package:

Wenseleers T, Vanderaa C (2026). *logconNMF: Log-Concave Nonnegative
Matrix Factorization with Automatic Rank Selection*. R package version
0.1.0.9000, <https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/>.

The [Authors and Citation
page](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/authors.html#citation)
also provides the citation in BibTeX format. Please also cite the
methodological sources linked in the help pages where relevant.

## Acknowledgements

OpenAI Codex, using GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, was used to optimize
and refactor code and help draft the documentation. The key ideas and
methodological decisions are the authors’ own, and the authors take full
responsibility for the work presented here.

# Package index

## Estimate point spread functions and deconvolve signals

- [`convKernel()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/convKernel.md)
  [`shiftKernel()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/convKernel.md)
  : Generate normalised 1-D convolution kernels (point-spread functions)
- [`convMatrix()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/convMatrix.md)
  : Make banded or rectangular convolution design matrices
- [`estimatePSF()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSF.md)
  : Estimate constant or time-varying point spread functions
- [`estimatePSFFromStd()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/estimatePSFFromStd.md)
  : Estimate a time-varying PSF matrix from an alkane ladder TIC
- [`l0glmBlindDeco()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/l0glmBlindDeco.md)
  : Alternating sparse L0 glm powered blind deconvolution
- [`l0glmSparseDeco()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/l0glmSparseDeco.md)
  : Sparse deconvolution with a fixed PSF via L0-penalised GLMs
- [`l0glmDecoEstKernel()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/reference/l0glmDecoEstKernel.md)
  : Estimate the PSF given a spike train estimate via L0-penalised GLMs

  estimate

# Articles

### Tutorials

- [Estimate
  PSFs](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/estimate-psf.md):

  Known convolution, blind kernel estimation and calibrated constant or
  time-varying point spread functions.

- [Sparse log-concave NMF with automatic best rank
  tuning](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/log-concave-nmf.md):

  Recover nonnegative profiles and loadings with flexible noise models,
  hard shape constraints and automatic rank selection.

- [Simultaneous log-concave NMF on 16 full
  chromatograms](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/simultaneous-nmf.md):

  Share spectra across aligned samples with log-concave profiles,
  missing compounds and flexible noise models.

### Algorithm and theory

- [Algorithms and theory for PSFs and sparse log-concave
  factorization](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/logconNMF/articles/algorithm.md):

  Likelihoods, initialization, shape constraints, rank objectives and
  mathematical pseudocode for single- and multisample models.
